about: Threadline brand data, version 1.0. Every rule in the brand book as structured data; American English. This edition defines no logo animation and no sound.
name: Threadline

revisions.changes: First edition of this brand book. The mark is a spool of thread, drawn from the name; the arch mark that came before it is retired. Adds a complete light theme, code colors, contrast pairs and the applications.

idea.line: An audit trail is one thread. You pull it to follow what happened.
explanation: By default, a database keeps only a record’s current values. It doesn’t remember what a value was before, or who changed it. Threadline puts every change on one timeline, in order, each tied to its actor: a person, or a part of your system such as a background job.
The mark is a spool with its loose end running free. The wound thread is the history already recorded; the loose end is where you start pulling. The name is the instruction: follow the line.

The spool is built from a few plain parts: a round disc at each end (the flanges) in Ink, a barrel between them, and the Stitch Blue thread wound on it. Nothing in it is a lock, a shield or an eye. Threadline helps people find what happened; it does not guard or watch.

positioning: An audit trail library for Phoenix apps. Threadline records every insert, update and delete in your PostgreSQL database, so you can open any record’s history and see what changed, who changed it and when.
job: Help me see what happened to a record in my database, in the words I already use.

audience.job: Add an audit trail to my Phoenix app without rewriting it.
audience.need: A setup that fits a normal Phoenix app: add `{:threadline, "~> 1.1.0"}`, run one migration that adds audit triggers to the tables they choose, and check which tables are audited.

audience.job: See who changed a record, what they changed and when.
audience.need: One place, Threadline Admin, to filter changes by database table, person or job, and date, open a record’s full history and copy its id into a support ticket.

audience.job: Find out whether Threadline records the changes we need to audit, and how we can review and export them.
audience.need: A plain account of what is recorded, which personal data is redacted or left out, how long audit history is kept and how to export it, and no claim Threadline can’t back up.

values.meaning: Name what people look for: the database table, the record, what changed, who changed it and when. Not “evidence plane” or “posture”.
Show the real id, the real timestamp and the real value. An audit trail that rounds a number up or down, or sums up a change, is not a true record.
Say what Threadline records and what it does not. Never “tamper-proof”, “immutable” or “compliant”.
People open Threadline Admin when something has gone wrong. Be steady and brief.
Audit history lives in the host app’s own database, and the host app decides who can open Threadline Admin. Threadline’s name and logo are never shown to the host app’s customers.

rules: The name is Threadline: one word, capital T. In code it is `threadline`.
Never run the thread through the word, and never put a shape behind the spool.
Insert, Update, Delete and Redacted are always written out. Their semantic colors back up the word; they never replace it.

logo.mark: A spool seen from slightly above: two round end discs (flanges) with an axle hole, thread in Stitch Blue wound as a spiral that sits on the lower disc, and the loose end peeling off the last turn toward the word. Every end disc and turn uses the same ellipse, and every overlap has the same gap.
logo.wordmark: Threadline, one word, capital T, in Familjen Grotesk SemiBold, outlined from the font so no live text is needed, with Th, re and ea kerned tighter. The spool sits to the left, sized so its thread band matches the letters’ stem; the gap is the n’s stem pitch, about half the capital height, and the spool is centered on the capitals.
logo.together: The spool and the word are one lockup. Do not rearrange them, resize one against the other or place the spool anywhere but at the left of the word.
logo.mono: One color is the same drawing in a single color: the gaps between the end discs, the turns and the loose thread carry the form, so nothing is redrawn. Ink on light, Fog on dark.
logo.small: Below 64 px the spool has its own simpler drawing: fewer turns of thread and wider gaps, so it still reads at small sizes, such as in a browser tab. The 16 and 32 px favicons use that simpler drawing, placed so its main edges land on whole pixels and its curves stay smooth. Below 16 px, do not use the mark.
logo.clear: Keep clear space on every side equal to a quarter of the lockup’s height, measured from the outermost edge of the lockup. Nothing enters it: no text, edge or other logo.
logo.minNote: On screen, the lockup is never narrower than 96 px and the mark never smaller than 16 px. In print, never narrower than 25 mm.
logo.theme: The logo has a version for each theme. On light, the spool’s end discs and the word are Ink; on dark, they are Fog. The thread is Stitch Blue on both. Use the version made for the background; do not make one by inverting the colors of the other.
logo.background: No shape behind it: the lockup sits directly on the page background. A photograph or screenshot behind the logo needs a calm area at least as wide as the lockup plus its clear space.
logo.retired: The arch mark is retired. It was an earlier attempt at a Threadline logo: an arc over a bar, and an arc between the d and the l in the wordmark. This edition replaces it with the spool, so do not use it. It read as a padlock shackle, a magnet or a staple, which is the wrong promise for an audit trail library.
misuse: Don’t stretch, squeeze or rotate the lockup.
Don’t recolor the thread or the word, or use Thread Blue for the thread.
Don’t put a tile, badge or any other shape behind the spool.
Don’t add the tagline, the descriptor or any text to the lockup.
Don’t run a line through the word, or draw the thread through the letters.
Don’t use the dark drawing on a light page, or the light drawing on a dark one.

onPhotography.head: On screenshots and photographs
rules: Place the lockup on a calm area at least as wide as the lockup and its clear space.
Use the light drawing on a light area and the dark drawing on a dark one. If neither reads well, move the logo.
Do not put a shape or a shadow behind it to make it read.

useByOthers: Hex packages, blogs, newsletters and conference sites may use the lockup unchanged to refer to Threadline.
Do not use it to suggest that Threadline endorses, certifies or audits another product.
Do not alter the logo, or build a new logo that uses the spool.

color.notes: Ratios are WCAG 2.2 contrast, computed from the hex values. A pair that passes here says nothing about a whole product built with it. Stitch Blue on Paper is 3.6:1: enough for a shape, not for text. Hairline and Slate Line only divide space and are never used for text.

display.use: The wordmark, headlines in books, slides and social cards, and page titles in docs.

messaging.pitch: Threadline is an audit trail library for Phoenix apps. It records every insert, update and delete in your PostgreSQL database, with who made each change and when, and adds Threadline Admin, where your team can follow what happened.
pillars: A PostgreSQL trigger on each audited table records every insert, update and delete in the same transaction that saves it.
Open any record to see every change ever made to it, or see the record as it was at any point in the past.
Audit history is stored in your own PostgreSQL database. Threadline Admin runs inside your app, and you decide who can open it and how they sign in.
messaging.tagline: Sentence case, with the period. It sits beside the logo, never in it.
boilerplate: One line: Hex, GitHub and package listings
An audit trail library for Phoenix that records every row change in PostgreSQL, so you can follow what happened.

Threadline is an open-source audit trail library for Elixir and Phoenix apps. It records each insert, update and delete in PostgreSQL, with who made it and when, and includes Threadline Admin, where your team can look up a record and see every change made to it, who made it and when.
Tamper-proof, immutable, compliant, certified, “audit log”, “powerful”, “seamless”, “next-generation”. Threadline records changes; whether that meets a regulation is for your team to decide.

rules: No status colors in code: no green, amber or red, so nothing in code looks like an insert, a delete, a redacted value or a changed field.
Module names and function heads stand out by weight (600), not by another color.
Syntax colors are for code blocks only. Inline code in a sentence is plain IBM Plex Mono on a chip, in every medium.
Use these colors where Threadline styles code: slides, social cards, blog posts and screenshots. GitHub and ExDoc color their own code; leave that alone.
Show code that matches the current release, not pseudo-code.

graphicElements.head: One line that connects things: the thread.
graphicElements.intro: The thread is the brand’s only graphic device. It is a thin Stitch Blue line that links items in order, the way a history links changes. It is used sparingly, and only where it links one item to the next.
items: A 2 px Stitch Blue vertical line with a small knot at each item, and no curl at the end. It joins the changes in one record’s history, or the steps on a docs page. Entries start on one grid, so the words beside each operation line up.
The thread’s last stretch: the line lifts slightly and ends in a flat cut, as the logo’s thread does leaving the spool. It closes the divider under a page header or a banner, once.
graphicElements.never: The thread never runs through text, never loops decoratively, never fills a background and never replaces the logo. One thread line per view.

legal: Threadline is released under the MIT license. The logo and this brand book are covered by the same license unless the repository says otherwise.
No trademark registration is claimed in this book, and none was searched. Use ™, not ®, only if the maintainers decide to claim the name.
Fonts are SIL Open Font License 1.1; their license texts ship in the assets folder.
contact: Questions about the brand and requests to use it: the Threadline maintainers, through the project’s issue tracker.
Approval: the maintainers approve any use that changes the logo or colors; unchanged use under these rules needs no approval.

notNeeded.why: Considered, not proposed. An audit trail library is trusted for being exact and calm, and a character pulls the other way.
The thread is the only graphic device. A pattern would compete with dense tables, where the data is the picture.
There is no honest photograph of “what happened in a database”. Real product pictures say it better.

notNeeded.item: A second typeface for the logo
notNeeded.why: The wordmark and the headlines are both set in Familjen Grotesk, so no other display face is needed.
In a dense table the data should carry the color. Rows stay on Graphite or Card White; color marks only the operation word.
Not defined in this edition. The brand has no motion or sound rules yet; see To review.

toReview.detail: Key terms (record, redacted, audited table, host app, Threadline Admin) are recommendations for the product’s own words too. Tell the maintainers which to change.

toReview.choice: The logo blue is Stitch Blue everywhere.
toReview.detail: The product draws its logo with the accent color. This book states the rule; the product’s logo component would need to change.

toReview.choice: Light-theme values come from the product’s light mode.
toReview.detail: Thread Blue Deep, Card White and Hairline were read from the product at the time of writing. Slate Text is new in this book and was never in the product.

toReview.choice: No motion and no sound yet.
toReview.detail: The logo has no animation and the brand has no sound. Both are possible next editions; neither is required to use this identity.

toReview.choice: An opaque square icon is not made.
toReview.detail: GitHub organization avatars and some platform icons need an opaque square. The logo files have no background shape, so the choice is left open.

toReview.choice: How people sign in, and the Admin logo.
toReview.detail: This book says the host app decides who can open Threadline Admin and how they sign in (its own login, single sign-on or a set username and password), and that a host app may replace the lockup with its own name and logo. The product lets the host app authorize access; it documents no logo setting, so that would need to be built.

toReview.choice: Threadline Admin is a new name.
toReview.detail: The product calls its UI the operator surface and mounts it at `/audit` in its examples. This book names it Threadline Admin; the product would need to follow.

notChecked: Name and trademark clearance were not searched; the name was kept. Code samples follow the README and were not run. Logo legibility was checked on one test sheet, not with people. Contrast is computed for the pairs listed here, not for a whole product. Print color was not proofed.
retired: The earlier arch mark and the arc between the d and the l, replaced by the spool.
The Thread Blue logo in the product: the logo thread is Stitch Blue.
The words “audit platform”, “evidence plane”, “operator surface”, “audit log”, “masked” and “Find, Verify, Prove”.
